case_studies.title: Harness-R1: Learning to Edit Executable Runtime Harnesses from Agent Failure Trajectories
case_studies.abstract: Agents built around large language models continually accumulate interaction trajectories during deployment, yet their behavior typically remains fixed. Beyond updating model weights, these trajectories can improve the agent harness that constructs context, mediates tools, validates actions, and recovers execution. We introduce Harness-R1, the first method, to our knowledge, that makes failure-conditioned, lifecycle-wide editing of an existing executable runtime a learned capability. It post-trains a dedicated harness engineer with online reinforcement learning so that its edits are optimized
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of improving agent behavior in large language models by introducing a method called Harness-R1, which builds a learned capability to edit executable runtime harnesses. The result is a more effective agent that can construct context, mediate tools, and recover from execution failures. This research may have implications for IT systems that rely on large language models.

Before deployment, these systems need to be verified against business requirements that govern workflow execution and data evolution. However, existing approaches do not provide such system-level guarantees, as they mainly constrain or analyse behaviour at the agent's interface level. The researchers formalised agentic systems and verified them against business requirements. This work is relevant to organisations using large language models in their workflows.

case_studies.title: A Security-Oriented Lifecycle Model for Large Language Model Systems
case_studies.abstract: Large language models are being integrated into critical infrastructure and enterprise workflows at unprecedented scale,yet the lifecycle frameworks governing their development and operations were designed for operational efficiency rather than security analysis. As a result, security-relevant activities such as data provenance verification, artifact signing, agentic permission control, and decommissioning are often left implicit or assumed to receive due care. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of security in large language models by creating a security-oriented lifecycle model, which provides a framework for secure development and operation of these models, resulting in improved security analysis and risk management. The researchers built a model that prioritizes security-relevant activities such as data provenance verification and artifact signing. This model helps to ensure the secure integration of large language models into critical infrastructure and enterprise workflows.

case_studies.title: Real-Time Detection and Repair of LLM Agent Failures
case_studies.abstract: LLM agents fail mid-episode -- they loop, cascade tool errors, drift off goal, fabricate results, or silently absorb corrupted content -- and the standard remedy, judging every step with a second LLM, costs more than the agent itself. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of LLM agent failures by detecting and repairing them in real-time, building a system that uses observable step telemetry to monitor agent performance, resulting in a cost-effective solution. The system was tested on 2,823 agent episodes across three frameworks and achieved promising results. This research aims to reduce the costs associated with LLM agent failures.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM agents, here is what to do: monitor step telemetry to detect potential failures, consider implementing a one-class echo-state-network ensemble with CUSUM alarms to reduce detection costs, and review your current remedy procedures to optimize agent performance.
case_studies.score_reasoning: While the paper's IT relevance is moderate, novelty is relatively low. There is some actionable value for IT engineers to consider, especially those working with LLMs, so that warrants a score above 0.

case_studies.title: From Bug Reports to Browser-Executable Procedures: An LLM-Driven Agent for Web GUI Bug Reproduction
case_studies.abstract: Reproducing web GUI bugs from natural-language bug reports is critical for software maintenance, but remains difficult because reports often lack prerequisites such as dependencies and input files. Existing bug reproduction techniques mainly target code units or mobile applications and lack end-to-end visual execution and validation for web GUIs. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of reproducing web GUI bugs from natural-language bug reports by building an agent system called ReBug, which reconstructs and executes browser-level reproduction procedures, resulting in improved bug reproduction accuracy. ReBug drives a real browser to validate bug reports, making it a useful tool for software maintenance. This research is relevant to IT work as it affects web application testing and maintenance.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage web applications, here is what to do: check your current bug reporting and testing processes, consider integrating ReBug or similar tools to improve bug reproduction accuracy, and review your testing infrastructure to ensure it can support browser-level execution and validation.

case_studies.title: HALT: Verification-Aware Stopping for Retrieval-Augmented Search Agents
case_studies.abstract: Retrieval-augmented search agents answer multi-hop questions by repeatedly issuing search queries and accumulating evidence. This creates a stopping problem: after the necessary evidence has appeared, further retrieval often adds cost, latency, and distracting context rather than useful information. We frame stopping as evidence coverage rather than generator confidence, and introduce HALT, a lightweight verification-aware policy that leaves the search agent unchanged. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of stopping retrieval-augmented search agents at the right time, by introducing HALT, a verification-aware policy that stops the search agent when enough evidence is gathered. The result is a reduction in cost, latency, and distracting context. This research is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on retrieval-augmented search agents and question answering systems.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novel algorithm for retrieval-augmented search agents, but its immediate practical application is unclear; low novelty since it's a solution to a specific problem with limited broader IT relevance; IT engineers may not see direct benefits from this.

case_studies.title: Self-Evolving Coding Agents
case_studies.abstract: Large language models are increasingly embedded in software engineering workflows as coding agents that can inspect repositories, invoke tools, execute tests, debug failures, and generate patches. Yet most existing agents remain largely static after deployment, even though software development is a dynamic, feedback-rich process in which repositories evolve, dependencies change, tests fail, and repair attempts leave reusable experience. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of static coding agents in software development by building self-evolving coding agents that can improve their future behavior. The researchers created a framework that allows coding agents to update themselves based on experience and feedback. The result is a more dynamic and adaptive coding agent that can better support software development workflows.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage software development workflows that use large language models as coding agents, here is what to do: assess your current agents' ability to evolve and improve, consider implementing a self-evolving framework, and monitor the impact on your development process. This flags a risk: if your org uses static coding agents, check for potential inefficiencies and errors that could be mitigated by self-evolving agents. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work outside of software development.

case_studies.title: LiveEvalBench: Toward Open-World Evaluation for Web Generation
case_studies.abstract: Large language models are increasingly capable of synthesizing executable frontend projects, yet existing benchmarks still treat web generation as a static evaluation problem. We argue that frontend artifacts demand a different paradigm: they are interactive rather than static, admit diverse yet equally valid implementations, and evolve faster than rigid pipelines can accommodate. To address these gaps, we present LiveEvalBench, an automated framework that reformulates web-generation evaluation as an agentic, adaptive, and extensible process. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluating web generation by large language models, building an automated framework called LiveEvalBench, and resulting in a more flexible and adaptive evaluation process. LiveEvalBench allows for the evaluation of interactive and dynamic frontend projects. This research is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on the evaluation of web generation by large language models, which is more relevant to software development and research.

Relevant to IT engineers as it involves large language models, which are used in many tools, but not directly relevant to infrastructure or security (9/33). Value lies in the ability to automate evaluation and improve LLMs but lacks a clear, specific use case. Scores 9/34 for potential to be used in the next 90 days.

case_studies.title: Interpretable Adaptive Sampling for LLM Test-Time Scaling
case_studies.abstract: Test-time scaling improves LLM reasoning by generating and aggregating multiple candidate answers, yet many pipelines use fixed per-query budgets that spend the same compute on easy and difficult prompts. These fixed budgets are also difficult to inspect because they do not explain why a given prompt receives a particular number of samples. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of inefficient test-time scaling in Large Language Models (LLMs) by building an adaptive sampling system that adjusts compute resources based on prompt complexity and model confidence, resulting in improved LLM reasoning. The system uses a lightweight fuzzy controller to map interpretable signals to a per-query sampling budget. This leads to more efficient use of compute resources.
